sections.heading: 1. List, stack and queue runtimes (slides 9 to 14)

blocks.md: Poon asks the **worst-case** runtime of every operation, for **two** builds of each ADT. Don't memorize the grid: each answer has a one-line reason, and the reason is what gets you the points on a variation.

rows: array: jump straight to slot i. Linked list: no index, walk from head i steps
array: adding at the front shifts every item right (or the array is full and must be copied). Linked list: relink two pointers, but finding index i first is a walk
**O(1)** at head / known node · O(n) by index or value
array: shift everything left to close the gap. Linked list: relink, once you're there
both keep a counter; nobody counts items
blocks.title: Lists (slide 10)

rows: array: write at top, except when full: copy everything into an array twice as big. That rare O(n) averages out to O(1)
the top is always the last filled index (array) or head (list)
blocks.title: Stacks (slide 12)

rows: write at tail; the array resize is the same story as the stack
move the **head index** forward instead of shifting everything left: that's the whole point of 'circular'
blocks.title: Queues (slide 14)

blocks.body: The **average cost per operation over a long run**, when most calls are cheap and a rare one is expensive. n pushes cost n writes plus copies of 1 + 2 + 4 + … < 2n items, so about 3n total: **O(1) each, amortized**.
Writing just 'O(1)' for an array push. Poon's answer is **'O(1) amortized, O(n) for resize'**: say both.

blocks.prompt: Why is dequeue O(1) on a circular array, when removing the front of a normal array is O(n)?
blocks.answer: Nothing shifts: the head index moves forward one slot (wrapping around at the end).

blocks.prompt: Linked list add at the tail is O(1). What does the list need for that to be true?
blocks.answer: A **tail pointer**. Without it you'd walk from head: O(n).

His practice problem, word for word in spirit: **write a loop invariant that holds before the loop condition is checked**, then prove it with the three parts.

blocks.title: The code (slide 16)
blocks.answer: result = a^i

blocks.body: **Before the loop condition is checked, result = aⁱ.** (After i trips through the loop, result has been multiplied by a exactly i times.)

rows: Before the first iteration, i = 0 and result = 1. a⁰ = 1, so the invariant holds.
Assume it holds at the start of an iteration: result = aᵏ (with i = k). The body does result = result · a = aᵏ · a = **aᵏ⁺¹**, and i becomes k + 1. So it holds for the next check.
The loop stops when i = p. The invariant still holds at that final check, so result = **aᵖ**, which is what's returned. The algorithm is correct.
blocks.title: The three parts, filled in

blocks.md: **How to find an invariant for any loop.** Ask: 'after i trips through the loop, what is true about the variable that builds the answer?' Write that with i in it. Then check: plug in i = 0 (should be the starting value) and i = the stopping value (should be the final answer). If both work, you have it.
blocks.label: think

blocks.body: Writing the invariant with the **final** value (result = aᵖ). That's only true at the end. It has to mention **i**, so it's true in the middle too.

blocks.prompt: For `s = 0; for i in range(n): s += a[i]`, what is the invariant before each check?
blocks.answer: s = a[0] + a[1] + … + a[i − 1] (the sum of the first i items). i = 0 gives the empty sum 0; i = n gives the whole sum.

sections.heading: 3. Prove a Big-O, and the growth table (slides 18 to 19)

blocks.body: f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist positive constants **c** and **n₀** such that **0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n₀**.

blocks.title: Slide 18: is 2n³ + 12 = O(n³)?
blocks.body:
1. Pick c a little bigger than the leading coefficient: **c = 3**.
2. Substitute: is 2n³ + 12 ≤ 3n³ ?
3. Simplify (subtract 2n³): is 12 ≤ n³ ?
4. Find where that starts: 2³ = 8 is too small, 3³ = 27 ≥ 12. So **n₀ = 3**.
5. Conclude: with c = 3 and n₀ = 3, 2n³ + 12 ≤ 3n³ for all n ≥ 3. **Yes, 2n³ + 12 = O(n³).**

blocks.md: **The recipe, every time:** (1) c = leading coefficient + 1, (2) substitute, (3) cancel the big term so only the leftovers remain, (4) find the first n where it's true: that's n₀, (5) say 'for all n ≥ n₀'. Any c and n₀ that work are correct; you don't need the smallest.
blocks.label: think

blocks.md: **Ω and Θ the same way.** For a floor, drop the small terms: 2n³ + 12 ≥ 2n³ for all n ≥ 1, so it's **Ω(n³)** with c = 2, n₀ = 1. Ceiling and floor are both n³, so it's **Θ(n³)**.

rows: halving, with a full pass per level
blocks.title: His growth table (slide 19), fastest to slowest

blocks.body: Stopping at 'c = 3 works' without **n₀**. The definition needs both constants, and 'for all n ≥ n₀'. Missing either costs points.

blocks.prompt: Prove 4n² + 50 = O(n²): give c and n₀.
blocks.answer: c = 5: 4n² + 50 ≤ 5n² ⇔ 50 ≤ n². 7² = 49 is too small, 8² = 64 works: **n₀ = 8**.

sections.heading: 5. Recurrences: read, substitute, draw the tree (slides 23 to 36)

blocks.md: Three skills, each one a likely detailed question: say a recurrence **in English**, prove a guess by **substitution**, and add up a **recursion tree** with the table.

rows: runtime for 1 problem of size n = runtime for **2** problems of size **n/2**
= runtime for 3 problems of size n/5, **plus 17 operations**
= runtime for 3 problems of size n/5, plus **4n** operations
= runtime for 2 problems of size n/2, plus **O(n)** operations (merge sort)
blocks.title: Read it out loud (slides 23 to 24)
Substitution: T(n) = T(n − 1) + n is O(n²) (slide 26)
blocks.body:
1. **Guess** O(n²): show T(n) ≤ cn² for all n ≥ n₀.
2. **Assume** it holds for n − 1: T(n − 1) ≤ c(n − 1)².
3. **Substitute** into the recurrence:
   T(n) = T(n − 1) + n
        ≤ c(n − 1)² + n
        = c(n² − 2n + 1) + n
        = cn² − 2cn + c + n
        = cn² − (2c − 1)n + c
4. **Prove** that's ≤ cn²: need −(2c − 1)n + c ≤ 0, i.e. (1 − 2c)n + c ≤ 0.
   (1 − 2c) must be negative. Pick **c = 1**: −n + 1 ≤ 0, true for all n ≥ 1. **n₀ = 1.** QED.
Step 2 on his slide is printed as T(n − 1) ≤ (n − 1)², without the c. Write it **with the c**: c(n − 1)². Step 3 uses it.

blocks.title: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + kn: fill out the table (slides 28 to 30)
How many levels? (slide 31)
blocks.body:
The base case is size 1. Level k has size n/2ᵏ, so
n/2ᵏ = 1 ⇒ n = 2ᵏ ⇒ log₂ n = k.
That's log₂ n levels **below** the root; **log₂ n + 1** including it.
Total = kn × (log₂ n + 1) = **O(n log n)**.
blocks.answer: O(n log n)

blocks.title: Add it up
blocks.body:
Levels: n/3ᵏ = 1 ⇒ k = log₃ n, so **log₃ n + 1** levels including the root.
Total = c(1 + 3 + 9 + … + 3ᵏ) = c(3ᵏ⁺¹ − 1)/2.
3ᵏ = n, so 3ᵏ⁺¹ = 3n: total = **c(3n − 1)/2 = Θ(n)**.
Check n = 9: c + 3c + 9c = 13c, and (27 − 1)/2 = 13. ✓
The master method agrees: a = 3, b = 3, n^(log₃ 3) = n beats f(n) = c, case 1, Θ(n).
blocks.answer: Θ(n)

blocks.md: **Why the rows differ.** In merge sort, nodes double and work halves, so every row is kn. Here nodes triple but each node's work stays c, so rows **grow** ×3 and the bottom row (n leaves) dominates. Which row dominates is exactly what the master method's three cases decide.
blocks.label: think

blocks.prompt: T(n) = T(n − 1) + 1 has how many levels, and what's the total?
blocks.answer: n levels (it subtracts 1, it doesn't halve), 1 work each: Θ(n).

sections.heading: 6. The master method, and when it doesn't apply (slides 39 to 43)

blocks.md: For **T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)**: compute **n^(log_b a)**, compare it with f(n), pick the case. Poon's three examples all use a = 4, b = 2, so n^(log₂ 4) = **n²**, and only f(n) changes.

rows: polynomially **smaller**: n = O(n^(2 − ε)) with ε = 1
polynomially **larger**: n³ = Ω(n^(2 + ε)) with ε = 1, **and** regularity holds
blocks.title: 4T(n/2) + f(n), three ways (slides 39, 40, 43)

blocks.body: **a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n)** for some constant **c < 1** and all large n. In words: the **next level's total work** (a calls, each doing f(n/b)) is at most a fraction of **this level's work**. The work shrinks geometrically going down, so the root's f(n) dominates.

blocks.title: Check regularity for 4T(n/2) + n³ (slide 43)
blocks.body:
a·f(n/b) = 4·(n/2)³ = 4·n³/8 = n³/2
Need n³/2 ≤ c·n³ ⇒ 1/2 ≤ c.
Pick **c = 1/2** (it's < 1). Regularity holds, so case 3: **Θ(n³)**.
blocks.answer: c = 1/2 works

columns: Why the master method does NOT apply
rows: the subproblem size isn't **n/b**: it subtracts instead of divides
n/log n is smaller than n, but only by a **log factor**, not polynomially: no ε > 0 makes n/log n = O(n^(1 − ε)). Not case 1, not case 2
f is polynomially larger but the work doesn't shrink level by level
blocks.title: 'Give examples where the master method does not apply' (slides 41 to 42)

blocks.md: **Why a log gap isn't enough.** Subtracting from the exponent (n^0.99) eventually beats dividing by log n, for any tiny ε. So n/log n sits **between** case 1 and case 2. Full-credit answer: '**does not apply**, because the gap is only logarithmic, not polynomial.'
blocks.label: think

blocks.body: Using case 3 without checking regularity. Poon shows the check on the slide, so he expects it in your answer.

blocks.prompt: T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n: which case and answer?
blocks.answer: n^(log₃ 9) = n². f = n is polynomially smaller (ε = 1): case 1, **Θ(n²)**.

sections.heading: 7. Heaps: fill in the ?s, and what happens if 14 → 3 (slides 46 to 52)

blocks.title: The slide's heap
blocks.body:
array: [16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1] (indexes 0 to 9)
index 1 holds 14: its children are at 3 (8) and 4 (7); its parent is at 0 (16).

blocks.md: **Slide 47's question: what happens if the 14 becomes a 3?** Now a[1] = 3 is smaller than its children, so the heap property breaks at index 1, and only there. The fix is **heapify(a, 1)**: let the 3 sink, swapping with the **larger** child each time.

frames.caption: heapify(a, 1, 10): a[1] = 3 may be smaller than a child. Both subtrees under it are already heaps, so only 3 is out of place.
Line 3: the children of index 1 are at 3 and 4. Line 4 starts with largest = 1.
Line 5: is the left child a[3] = 8 bigger than a[1] = 3? **Yes**. Line 6: largest = 3.
Line 7: is the right child a[4] = 7 bigger than a[3] = 8? **No**.
Line 9: largest = 3, not 1. Line 11 swaps a[1] = 3 with a[3] = 8: the bigger child moves up.
Line 12: i = 3. The sinking value, 3, is now at index 3. Back to the top of the loop to check its new children.
Line 3: the children of index 3 are at 7 and 8. Line 4 starts with largest = 3.
Line 5: is the left child a[7] = 2 bigger than a[3] = 3? **No**.
Line 7: is the right child a[8] = 4 bigger than a[3] = 3? **Yes**. Line 8: largest = 8.
Line 9: largest = 8, not 3. Line 11 swaps a[3] = 3 with a[8] = 4: the bigger child moves up.
Line 12: i = 8. The sinking value, 3, is now at index 8. Back to the top of the loop to check its new children.
Line 3: the children of index 8 are at 17 and 18 (both past the end of the heap). Line 4 starts with largest = 8.
Line 9: largest is still 8, so 3 is at least as big as its children. Line 10 returns: the heap is fixed.

blocks.title: The three steps, as you'd write them
blocks.body:
heapify(a, 1): children 8 (index 3) and 7 (index 4). Max child 8 swaps with 3.
heapify(a, 3): children 2 (index 7) and 4 (index 8). Max child 4 swaps with 3.
heapify(a, 8): index 8 has no children (2·8 + 1 = 17 > 9). Base case, done.
Result: [16, 8, 10, 4, 7, 9, 3, 2, 3, 1]

rows: one value sinks down one path; the tree's height is log n
most nodes are near the bottom and sink only a level or two; the sum works out to < 2n
n times: swap the root to the end, heapify(0)
it sorts inside the same array
swapping the root to the end jumps it over equal items
add at the end, swap **up** past smaller parents
take a[0], move the last item to 0, heapify(0)
blocks.title: Slide 52, with the reasons

blocks.body: Swapping with the **first** child instead of the **larger** one. If you swap 3 with 7 instead of 8, then 7 is the parent of 8: still broken.

blocks.prompt: Why is buildHeap O(n) and not O(n log n), even though it calls heapify n/2 times?
blocks.answer: Most of those calls are on nodes near the bottom, which can sink only 0 or 1 levels. Only the root can sink log n.

sections.heading: 8. Hash tables: a good hash function, and chaining runtimes (slides 54 to 56)

rows: the same key always gives the same slot (or you could never find it again)
hashing is done on every insert and search; a slow hash kills the O(1)
spreads keys evenly across all the slots, so chains stay short
blocks.title: What makes a good hash function? (slide 54)

blocks.body: **Every key is equally likely to land in any slot, independently of where the other keys went.** It's an assumption that makes the math work: with it, every chain has about the same length, α.
**α = n / m**: elements in the table divided by slots. That's the **average chain length**.

rows: hash to the slot, add to that chain
when α gets too big, make a bigger table and re-insert everything
resizes are rare: their cost spread over all inserts is constant
blocks.title: Chaining, assuming SUHA (slide 56)

blocks.md: **Why is O(α) the same as O(1)?** Because the table resizes whenever α passes a limit, so α never grows with n. It stays below a constant (like 0.75).

blocks.body: Forgetting the assumption. Without SUHA (a bad hash function that sends everything to one slot), search is **O(n)**.

blocks.prompt: What does SUHA assume, in one sentence?
blocks.answer: Any key is equally likely to hash to any slot, independent of the other keys.

sections.heading: 9. BSTs: why, traversals, insert, runtimes (slides 59 to 69)

columns: If hash tables are ~O(1), why BSTs?
rows: 'all products priced 20 to 50', 'orders between two dates'. A hash table has no order, so it scans everything: O(n)
'cheapest product', 'latest review'. Hash table: full scan, O(n). BST: walk left (or right): O(h)
blocks.title: Slide 59
Traverse 10(5(3, 7), 15) (slides 60 to 63)
blocks.body:
In-order   (left, node, right): 3, 5, 7, 10, 15   ← sorted
Pre-order  (node, left, right): 10, 5, 3, 7, 15
Post-order (left, right, node): 3, 7, 5, 15, 10

blocks.md: **A trick for traversals by hand.** Pre-order: write a node the **first** time you pass it going around the tree. In-order: when you pass **under** it. Post-order: the **last** time, on the way back up.

blocks.md: **Slide 66: where would we insert 19?** Walk down like a search: 19 > 15 go right, 19 > 18 go right, 19 < 20 go left, 20's left is empty: **19 becomes 20's left child**.

frames.caption: insert(root, 19). A new key always becomes a LEAF. Walk down exactly like search, until the spot is empty.
19 ≥ 15: go right.
19 ≥ 18: go right.
19 < 20: go left. 20.left is empty, so that's where 19 goes.
root is None: line 3 makes a new Node(19) and returns it. The caller stores it in 20.left.
Every call returns its root, so each parent re-links the same child it had (nothing changes above the new leaf). Still a BST: the in-order is still sorted.

rows: recursion follows the BST rule until it hits **null**: the insertion point
make the new node, not linked yet, and **return a pointer to it**
the new node's **parent** gets that pointer and stores it in its left or right child: now it's linked
every ancestor gets back its own unchanged child pointer and **blindly overwrites** it with the same value: no structural change

one path from the root down

blocks.title: Runtime analysis (slide 69)

blocks.md: **What's the worst case, and what causes it?** h can be **n − 1**: the tree is a **chain** (a linked list in disguise), and everything becomes **O(n)**. It happens when keys are inserted in **sorted (or reverse-sorted) order**: every new key goes to the same side. Balanced: h ≈ log n, everything **O(log n)**.

blocks.body: Saying 'BST search is O(log n)'. It's **O(h)**: O(log n) only when the tree is balanced. That gap is exactly why AVL trees exist.

blocks.prompt: Why does an in-order walk of a BST come out sorted?
blocks.answer: Left subtree (all smaller), then the node, then the right subtree (all bigger), at every node.

sections.heading: 10. AVL trees: draw the rotations, fill in the strategy (slides 71 to 76)

blocks.title: rightRotate(10) and leftRotate(10) on the slide's tree (slides 71 to 72)

frames.caption: The slide's tree: 10 on top, 1 on the left, 20 on the right, and 15 under 20 on the left. Two separate questions: what does rightRotate(10) give, and what does leftRotate(10) give?
**rightRotate(10).** x = 10, y = x.left = 1. temp = y.right = nothing (1 has no right child).

y.right = x and x.left = temp: 1 goes on top, 10 becomes 1's right child, and 10's left (it was 1) becomes temp, which is empty. The tree leans even further right now. That's fine: the question only asks for the shape.
**leftRotate(10)** (on the ORIGINAL tree). x = 10, y = x.right = 20. temp = y.left = 15: the middle piece that changes parents.
y.left = x and x.right = temp: 20 goes on top, 10 becomes 20's left child, and 15 moves over to be 10's RIGHT child. 15 is still between 10 and 20, so the BST order holds.
Check either answer with an in-order walk: both rotations keep it 1, 10, 15, 20. A rotation never changes the sorted order, only who is on top.

blocks.title: Both answers
blocks.body:
rightRotate(10): 1 on top → 1 (right: 10 (right: 20 (left: 15)))
leftRotate(10):  20 on top → 20 (left: 10 (left 1, right 15))
The rule: the child on the rotation's side comes up; the middle subtree (temp) changes parents.
blocks.answer: rightRotate → 1 on top · leftRotate → 20 on top

rows: standard BST search, then insert the leaf: **O(log n)**
for each node on the path: update **H = 1 + max(H(left), H(right))**, rebalance if needed
same, using the deletion LL / LR / RR / RL cases
blocks.title: Fill in the ?s: insert and delete strategy

blocks.md: **Why O(log n) is guaranteed:** the AVL rule (|B| ≤ 1 at every node) keeps the height at most about 1.44 log n, so 'one path down' is always short. A rotation is a few pointer changes: O(1).

blocks.body: Rotating the **wrong way**. rightRotate brings the **left** child up; leftRotate brings the **right** child up. Say it once before you draw.

blocks.prompt: After an AVL insert, at most how many rotation sets are needed? After a delete?
blocks.answer: Insert: at most one (single or double). Delete: up to O(log n), because a rotation can shorten a subtree and unbalance an ancestor.

blocks.md: The real exam's shape. **No notes, no scratch paper**: answer on the page, like Monday. Short answers first (one or two sentences each; flip each card when you've said your answer out loud), then the five **detailed** questions. They're the 'Do it yourself' boxes in sections 2 (invariant), 3 (Big-O proof), 6 (master method), 7 (heap extract) and 10 (AVL inserts). Write each one on paper before you open the solution.

blocks.prompt: 1. Worst-case runtime of get(i) on a linked list, and why?
blocks.answer: O(n): there's no index, so you walk from head i steps.

blocks.prompt: 2. Array-based stack push: what's the runtime?
blocks.answer: O(1) amortized; O(n) on the push that triggers a resize (copy into a bigger array).

blocks.prompt: 3. Name the three parts of a loop invariant proof.
blocks.answer: Initialization, maintenance, termination.

blocks.prompt: 4. Is heap sort stable? Why or why not?
blocks.answer: No: swapping the root to the end can jump it over an equal item.

blocks.prompt: 5. What is the runtime of buildHeap?
blocks.answer: O(n): most nodes sit near the bottom and sink only a little.

blocks.prompt: 6. Give two reasons to use a BST instead of a hash table.
blocks.answer: Range queries and min/max (anything needing order): a hash table must scan everything, O(n).

blocks.prompt: 7. What does the simple uniform hashing assumption assume?
blocks.answer: Any key is equally likely to hash to any slot, independently of the others.

blocks.prompt: 8. Quicksort's worst case: runtime, and what input causes it (last-item pivot)?
blocks.answer: O(n²), on already sorted (or reverse-sorted) input.

blocks.prompt: 9. Which comparison sorts are in place?
blocks.answer: Insertion sort, heap sort, quicksort. (Merge sort needs O(n) extra.)

blocks.prompt: 10. What does a plain BST look like in its worst case, and what causes it?
blocks.answer: A chain, height n − 1, so operations are O(n). Caused by inserting keys in sorted order.

exercises.title: Detailed 1: loop invariant
hints: Ask: after i trips through the loop, what does s hold?
Check your sentence at i = 0 (s should be 0) and at i = a.length (s should be the answer).
Maintenance: assume it at i = k, run the body once, show it for k + 1.
solution: **Invariant:** before the loop condition is checked, s = a[0] + a[1] + … + a[i − 1] (the sum of the first i items).
**Initialization:** before the first iteration i = 0 and s = 0, the sum of zero items. Holds.
**Maintenance:** assume s = a[0] + … + a[k − 1] when i = k. The body does s = s + a[k], so s = a[0] + … + a[k], and i becomes k + 1. Holds for the next check.
**Termination:** the loop stops when i = a.length = n. The invariant gives s = a[0] + … + a[n − 1], the sum of every item, which is returned. Correct.
exercises.why: Same shape as Poon's power(a, p) example on slide 16.

exercises.title: Detailed 2: prove a Big-O
exercises.prompt: Prove that 4n² + 50 = O(n²) using the formal definition. Give c and n₀.
hints: Pick c one more than the leading coefficient.
Cancel the 4n² from both sides.
Find the first whole n where what's left is true.
solution: Definition: f(n) = O(g(n)) if there are positive c, n₀ with 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
Let **c = 5**. Is 4n² + 50 ≤ 5n²? Subtract 4n²: is 50 ≤ n²?
With c = 5 and n₀ = 8, 4n² + 50 ≤ 5n² for all n ≥ 8. So 4n² + 50 = O(n²).
exercises.why: Slide 18's recipe. Any working c and n₀ get full credit.

exercises.title: Detailed 3: master method, three times
exercises.prompt:
Solve each with the master method, or say why it doesn't apply.
(a) T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n
(b) T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
(c) T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n²
(d) T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/log n
hints: Compute n^(log_b a) first for each.
(c) is case 3: check regularity, a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) with c < 1.
(d): is the gap polynomial?
solution: (a) a = 9, b = 3: n^(log₃ 9) = n². f = n is polynomially smaller (ε = 1). Case 1: **Θ(n²)**.
(b) a = 2, b = 2: n^(log₂ 2) = n. f = n is equal. Case 2: **Θ(n log n)**.
(c) n^(log₂ 2) = n. f = n² is polynomially larger (ε = 1). Regularity: 2·(n/2)² = n²/2 ≤ c·n² with c = 1/2 < 1. Holds. Case 3: **Θ(n²)**.
(d) n^(log₂ 2) = n. n/log n is smaller than n only by a log factor, not polynomially. **The master method does not apply.**
exercises.why: Poon's slides 39 to 43 in one question.

exercises.title: Detailed 4: extract from a max-heap
exercises.prompt: A max-heap is stored as [20, 18, 15, 9, 12, 10, 7, 2] (0-based). Trace one extract(): what does it return, and what is the array afterwards? Show each swap.
hints: The answer is the root. Then move the LAST item to index 0.
Sink it: swap with the LARGER child each time.
Children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the heap is one item shorter now.
solution: Return a[0] = **20**. Move the last item (2) to index 0; the heap is now 7 items: [2, 18, 15, 9, 12, 10, 7].
heapify(0): children 18 (index 1) and 15 (index 2). Larger is 18: swap → [18, 2, 15, 9, 12, 10, 7].
heapify(1): children 9 (index 3) and 12 (index 4). Larger is 12: swap → [18, 12, 15, 9, 2, 10, 7].
heapify(4): children would be 9 and 10, past the end (size 7). Done.
Result: **[18, 12, 15, 9, 2, 10, 7]**. O(log n): at most one swap per level.
exercises.why: Slide 78's 'trace insert and extract on a priority queue'.

exercises.title: Detailed 5: AVL inserts
exercises.prompt: Insert 10, 20, 30, 25, 28 in that order into an empty AVL tree. Name every rotation case and draw the final tree.
hints: After each insert, go back up and compute B = H(left) − H(right) at each node.
The case is the two steps from the unbalanced node toward the new key.
A zig-zag (LR or RL) needs two rotations.
solution: 10, 20: no problem.
30: at 10, B = −1 − 1 = −2. Path right, right: **RR** → leftRotate(10). Tree: 20 (10, 30).
25: goes 20 → 30 → left of 30. Every |B| ≤ 1. No rotation.
28: goes 20 → 30 → 25 → right of 25. At 30, B = 1 − (−1) = **+2**. Path from 30: left (25), then right (28): **LR** → leftRotate(25), then rightRotate(30). 28 comes up with 25 and 30 as its children.
exercises.why: Slide 74's strategy, and the HW 13 shape.

exercises.title: Regularity, in words
exercises.prompt: What does the regularity condition a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n), c < 1, guarantee?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **Geometric decay**: each level does at most c < 1 times the work of the one above.

choices.text: The work shrinks by a constant fraction at each level down, so the root dominates
choices.feedback: Yes: next level's total ≤ a fraction of this level's.

choices.text: The tree has log n levels
The leaves do most of the work

exercises.title: Why BSTs
exercises.prompt: Which task is O(n) with a hash table but O(h) with a BST?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **Min/max and range queries**: the hash table has no order.

choices.feedback: Yes: a hash table has no order, so it scans every key.
Hash lookup is O(1) on average.
Hash delete is O(1) on average.
